short: The accepted sources of valid knowledge, such as perception, inference and testimony.
beginner: Pramana means a reliable way of knowing. Indian philosophers argued about how many there are: some accept only perception, others add reasoning, reliable words, comparison and more.
what: A pramana is a means of acquiring valid knowledge (prama). Every Indian school had to state which pramanas it accepts, because this determines what can be known and argued. Charvaka accepts perception alone; Buddhist logicians accept perception and inference; Sankhya and Yoga add testimony; Nyaya adds comparison; Mimamsa and Vedanta add postulation and non-cognition. For Vedic schools, scripture (shabda) is the decisive source on matters beyond the senses.
scholar: Nyaya Sutra 1.1.3 lists perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), comparison (upamana) and testimony (shabda). Prabhakara Mimamsa adds arthapatti (postulation); Kumarila and Advaita add anupalabdhi (non-cognition), giving six. Debates concern svatah-pramanya (intrinsic validity, Mimamsa) versus paratah-pramanya (extrinsic validity, Nyaya), the structure of inference (the five-membered syllogism, vyapti), and whether scripture is authorless (apaurusheya) or authored by God.

perspectives.view: Nyaya accepts four pramanas and developed the classical theory of inference; it holds that knowledge is validated by its fit with successful action.
Mimamsa holds knowledge to be intrinsically valid unless defeated, and treats the authorless Veda as the sole source for dharma; Kumarila accepts six pramanas, Prabhakara five.
Advaita accepts six pramanas for worldly knowledge and holds that the Upanishads alone reveal Brahman, while noting that ultimately the Self is self-evident rather than an object of any pramana.
Buddhist epistemologists such as Dignaga and Dharmakirti accept only perception and inference, and reject scripture as an independent pramana.
Charvaka accepts only perception, questioning whether inference can ever be certain, and so rejects unseen realities such as rebirth.
Jain thought divides knowledge into direct and indirect kinds, and pairs pramana with nayas (partial standpoints).
Sankhya and Yoga accept perception, inference and reliable testimony.
